I can give you a video of me shooting a three pointer behind my back… It just may take me six months to get the right footage, but I assure you those 5 seconds will be real!

There were many different set ups and hence many different cuts and, if you think about the logistics, even if the robot could get each set up right on the first take, there would still need to be several sessions of shooting. The table cloth gimmick looks impressive, but all you need to control for is speed and angle, no fancy robotics needed.

Notice how sterile the environment is. Not a continuity error to be seen. Even if this was achieved without teleoperation, perhaps the shirt folding doesn’t generalize to any other fabric types, colors, or sizes. I’m not saying it’s fake, I’m just saying if this was a magic trick I have a pretty good idea of how the magician did it.

comments.author: @OmicronChannel
comments.text:
Let's assume the demo is real. What could be the gaps?

1. Required computing power: I wonder how much computing power is needed to generalize tasks. Do you need a supercomputer? This would drive up costs.

2. Reliability of a robot: How reliable is a robot that has been generalized for different tasks? Just recall, we don't even have reliable agents from large language models (LLMs). How could this then be possible for real-world agentic behavior by robots?

3. Related to point 2: Insurance What kind of insurance would be needed to have such a robot in a household, doing things unsupervised on its own? Remember that complete autonomous driving has still not been achieved.

If such generalization were possible, I assume that such robots would first be introduced in industry, not initially in consumer households. Thus, there is surely time to observe how reliable these promises are.

comments.author: @ClayMann
comments.text:
The design of this seems to be very dated compared to some of the others like Figure01 and the new Atlas. They all seem to be displaying a very similar, almost cookie cutter framework now of excellent LLM/virtual training going on that's giving them a real turbo boost compared to anything we've seen before. But they are all still very primitive in how they navigate our world whether walking around like little old men or doing some tasks that are so staged you just have to assume they can't actually practically do any of this yet. If they could, they'd just let one loose in a demo apartment with reporters allowed to watch or ask the robots to do stuff. I'm not being too mean here. I see the leap forward in just 2 years. This year has seen more progress in robotics than in my entire lifetime. So I'm hoping 2025 sees some really special things happening without staging or perfectly simple setups. 

One thing I'd love to see that is remarkably absent with all this new innovation. Pet like robots. Much smaller dog/cat sized things not bipedal. Perhaps balancing or just on regular wheels. where are all the cool new robots for the fun of it? The only ones I see googling around have been around for years and are either as small as your hand that can do almost nothing but can be fun. Especially with programming in mind for children but I want to see the LLM/virtual training leaps forward for pet robots too. Or robots just scaled down where you might even imagine they could be affordable to actually buy. Can anyone seriously look at this robot in this video and imagine buying it in the next few years?

comments.author: @Urgelt
comments.text:
We need to stop being impressed by teleoperated 'robots.'

The Chinese demo is teleoperated - either in real time using sensors focused on a human, or recorded and replayed in a carefully curated environment.

This is the conceptual differentiator: forget what you see it do. Consider what you do not see it do. Put the robot into an uncurated environment and give it tasks it doesn't have a script for.

Be impressed by Tesla's FSD. It does not require a curated pre-mapped route. It can successfully drive a route it has never before encountered, in weather, at night. That is AI. Optimus uses the same AI architecture and will soon perform assigned tasks on a factory floor it is encountering for the first time.

Heinlein tried to give us a vocabulary to differentiate teleoperation from robots. Robots, as he envisioned them, were capable of making decisions and following high-level conceptual instructions. Waldos were teleoperated machines. Alas, the later term did not stick. Everything now is a robot. And hucksters are using teleoperation to fool investors.
